prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay about the Erie Canal and what it changed
raw:
The Erie Canal is the most dangerous success in American history, and I say that as someone who loves it. I have biked the towpath from Albany to Buffalo twice. I have stood at Lockport, where Nathan Roberts's flight of five paired locks lifted boats sixty feet up the Niagara Escarpment, and felt the specific dizziness of looking at a staircase built for water. But I think the usual story about the canal, the one on the plaques, gets its meaning almost exactly backward. The canal did not prove that bold public investment pays. It proved that geography pays, and then it let a generation of politicians mistake one for the other.

Start with the numbers everyone quotes, because they are real. Before 1825, moving a ton of flour from Buffalo to New York City cost something like a hundred dollars and took the better part of three weeks. After the canal opened, the cost fell to about ten dollars, and the trip took around eight days. The state spent roughly seven million dollars on 363 miles of ditch, four feet deep and forty feet wide at the surface, climbing through 83 locks. Tolls paid off the debt in about a decade. Rochester went from a mill village of about 1,500 people in 1820 to more than 9,000 in 1830. New York City, which had been jostling with Philadelphia and Baltimore, pulled away from both and never looked back.

Jefferson had called the idea "little short of madness" in 1809, and the plaques love that line, because it makes DeWitt Clinton look like a visionary and Jefferson look like a fussy Virginian who couldn't imagine the future. But Jefferson was mostly right. A 363-mile canal through the American interior was madness almost everywhere. It worked in New York because of a quirk in the continent: the Mohawk River had cut the only water-level gap through the Appalachian chain anywhere between Georgia and Maine. The summit level between the Hudson and Lake Erie sits at a little over 500 feet. That is a gentle rise. You can walk it without noticing. Clinton's genius was recognizing a gift that the Ice Age had already wrapped. The engineers deserve their credit too. Benjamin Wright and James Geddes were surveyors who taught themselves the trade on the job, and Canvass White found the limestone near Chittenango that made hydraulic cement possible. But the essential fact was a hole in the mountains, and New York happened to own it.

Now look at what everyone else learned. Pennsylvania watched New York's toll receipts and panicked, and in 1826 it began the Main Line of Public Works to connect Philadelphia to Pittsburgh. There was no Mohawk gap in Pennsylvania. There was the Allegheny Front, which the Main Line crossed on the Allegheny Portage Railroad, a series of ten inclined planes on which stationary steam engines winched canal boats, sometimes in sections, up and over the mountain. I have walked the remains of Plane No. 6 near Hollidaysburg. It is a magnificent and slightly insane piece of work, and it lost money from the start. The state eventually sold the whole system to the Pennsylvania Railroad in 1857 for seven and a half million dollars, a fraction of what it had cost.

Indiana went further. In 1836 it passed the Mammoth Internal Improvement Act and committed about ten million dollars to canals, roads, and railroads, a sum close to a sixth of the state's entire wealth. By 1841 Indiana was in default. So were Illinois, Michigan, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and several others. British bondholders were furious and stayed furious for years, and states rewrote their constitutions to forbid the very kind of borrowing that had built the Erie. The canal's real institutional legacy, in other words, was a wave of debt-limit clauses written by people who had been burned trying to copy it.

None of this makes the canal less important. It made New York the gateway to the Great Lakes, so the grain of Ohio and Michigan flowed east to Manhattan rather than south to New Orleans, and that probably mattered for which way the Old Northwest leaned in 1861. It turned upstate New York into the Burned-over District, a corridor so crowded with new people and new money that it produced Joseph Smith in Palmyra, the Oneida Community, and the Seneca Falls convention within a few decades of one another. Ideas traveled at the speed of a mule, which turned out to be fast enough.

But the lesson the plaques teach, that a state with nerve can dig its way to greatness, is the lesson that bankrupted Indiana. The more accurate lesson is less flattering and more useful. Infrastructure pays when it follows the grain of the land and the grain of existing trade. The Erie was a shortcut cut along a path that commerce already wanted to take. Most of its imitators were attempts to make commerce go where it had no reason to go, and the bondholders found out the difference.

When I ride the towpath now, past locks where a few pleasure boats wait on a summer afternoon, I don't think about vision. I think about how lucky Clinton was to be governor of the one state where his idea could work.
